content:
Squares and Square Roots is the most pattern-rich chapter of Class 8. Unit digits, odd-number ladders, Pythagorean triplets — the IMO loves it because strong students finish these questions in seconds while everyone else multiplies. Start by testing the ground. The free IMO Class 8 Square Roots online test below asks 10 exam-pattern MCQs and scores them on the spot. Each explanation shows the intended one-minute route.

What the IMO asks from Square Roots in Class 8

  • Spotting perfect squares by unit digit and trailing zeros.
  • Patterns: 1 + 3 + 5 + … and squares of numbers ending in 5.
  • Pythagorean triplets from 2m, m² − 1, m² + 1.
  • Square roots by prime factorisation and by long division.
  • Smallest multiplier or divisor that produces a perfect square.

Key facts and formulas to revise first

  • A perfect square never ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8 — and never in an ODD number of zeros.
  • The sum of the first n odd numbers is n²: that is why 1 + 3 + … + 19 = 100.
  • Between n² and (n + 1)² sit exactly 2n non-square numbers.
  • For m = 6, the triplet 2m, m² − 1, m² + 1 gives 12–35–37.

Mistakes that cost Olympiad marks

  • Simplifying √(a² + b²) to a + b — 3-4-5 exists precisely because that fails.
  • Halving a number instead of taking its square root.
  • Finding the right multiplier but forgetting to report the NEW square root.

questions.q: If n is a natural number such that n² has 9 as its units digit, then the units digit of n must be:
questions.explanation: We need units digit d such that d² ends in 9. Checking: 3² = 9 (units digit 9) and 7² = 49 (units digit 9). No other single digit squared ends in 9. So the units digit of n is 3 or 7.

questions.q: If (n + 1)² - n² = 101, then the value of n is:
questions.explanation: (n + 1)² - n² = n² + 2n + 1 - n² = 2n + 1. Setting 2n + 1 = 101 gives 2n = 100, so n = 50.

questions.q: The number of perfect squares between 1 and 1000 (inclusive) that are divisible by both 4 and 9 is:
questions.explanation: A number divisible by both 4 and 9 is divisible by lcm(4, 9) = 36. A perfect square divisible by 36 must have n divisible by 6 (since 36 = 6²). So n = 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 give n² = 36, 144, 324, 576, 900 — all at most 1000

questions.q: The square root of 1764, found by prime factorisation, is:
Between which two consecutive integers does √(78) lie?
A perfect square has 12 digits. The number of digits in its square root is:
questions.explanation: For a number with n digits, its square root has ceil(n/2) digits. For n = 12: ceil(12/2) = 6. The smallest 12-digit number is 10¹¹ and √(10¹¹) = 316227... (6 digits); the largest is just under 10¹² and √(10¹² - 1) = 9999
